content.text: Tides are the regular rise and fall of sea levels, driven mainly by the gravitational pull of the Moon and, to a lesser extent, the Sun. As the Earth rotates, coastal waters bulge toward whichever celestial body is pulling hardest, creating high tides, while the opposite side of the planet experiences a corresponding bulge caused by inertia, which produces a second high tide. Between these peaks, water levels drop to low tides. Most coastlines experience two high and two low tides roughly every twenty-five hours, though some locations see only one of each per day. When the Sun and Moon align during new and full moons, their combined gravity produces unusually high spring tides, whereas the weaker tides occurring when they sit at right angles are called neap tides. Local geography, including the shape of bays, the depth of the seafloor, and the width of continental shelves, can greatly amplify or dampen these effects. Tides shape coastal ecosystems, influence navigation and fishing, and affect the movement of sediment and nutrients along shorelines.
